title: Input-sparsity relative spectral low-rank approximation
formal: Is there a randomized algorithm and absolute constants \(C,b>0\) that, for every real \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\), integer \(1\leq k<n\) and rational \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\), returns \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) with orthonormal columns such that \[\|A-ZZ^{\mathsf T}A\|_2\leq(1+\varepsilon)\min_{\operatorname{rank}(B)\leq k}\|A-B\|_2\] with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(C\operatorname{nnz}(A)+Cn(k/\varepsilon)^b\) operations?
why: Relative spectral approximation protects every direction of a compressed linear operator, making it useful where a small average error is insufficient. Resolving the question would determine whether this stronger guarantee can share the basic input-reading cost of fast Frobenius approximation, without rank or accuracy multiplying the sparse-data term.
status_note: Open in Woodruff’s 2014 survey and explicitly connected to an algorithmic frontier by the checked 2021 work. A bounded primary-source search on 13 September 2026 did not identify a resolution for arbitrary matrices with the stated strict running time; no exhaustive current-status certification is claimed.

importance.reason: A central runtime frontier in randomized numerical linear algebra, separating worst-direction compression guarantees from aggregate-error guarantees for arbitrary sparse matrices.

sentences: Spectral low-rank approximation seeks a rank-k representation whose largest directional error is near the best possible.
The source asks for a relative-error guarantee in time equal to reading the nonzero matrix entries plus a term linear in n and polynomial in k over epsilon.
That speed is available in the cited comparison for Frobenius error, which aggregates squared errors instead of controlling the worst direction.
The spectral target is therefore substantially stronger.
A solution would make sparse-matrix compression fast while protecting against a large error concentrated in one singular direction.

definitions: The matrix is given as a list of its nonzero entries, each with its row index, column index and real value; unspecified entries are zero and index pairs do not repeat. The integer \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) is the length of this list. The spectral norm is \(\|D\|_2=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Dx\|_2\). For singular values \(\sigma_1(A)\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n(A)\geq0\), the optimum on the right is \(\sigma_{k+1}(A)\). Orthonormality means \(Z^{\mathsf T}Z=I_k\), so \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}\) is an orthogonal projection of rank \(k\). The output is the explicit matrix \(Z\); forming the generally dense product \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}A\) is not required. All real input matrices are included, with no gap, conditioning, spectral-decay, positivity or distributional promise. If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq k\), the required residual is exactly zero on a successful run. The selected arithmetic model is a uniform real RAM with unit-cost addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root of a nonnegative value, real comparison, and indexed memory access. Registers store exact reals or integer indices; integer indexing arithmetic is charged, and no real-to-integer floor or bit extraction is a free primitive. Independent fair random bits and independent standard normal real samples are available at unit cost. This explicitly adopts the ideal arithmetic and sampling convention used in randomized numerical linear algebra; bit complexity is not the target. The operation bound includes reading the input, all preprocessing, random sampling and writing the output, and must hold on every random run. Only correctness may fail with probability at most one third, separately for each fixed input. A single algorithm and the same constants work for all parameters; \(n\geq2\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proofs of its probability guarantee and stated arithmetic running time, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The coefficient of the nonzero-entry term must be an absolute constant: multiplying that term by k, inverse accuracy or logarithms of n misses the target. Frobenius-norm error, additive spectral error, extra output rank, or a bound conditional on a singular-value gap does not establish the displayed claim.

context_blocks.text: Woodruff’s Open Question 1 asks whether the input-sparsity bound for relative Frobenius approximation can also give the relative spectral projection guarantee in Equation (65). The card makes the arithmetic model, success probability and output representation explicit; it retains the square-matrix target.

The Frobenius norm sums squared errors over all entries, whereas the spectral norm controls the largest error in a unit direction. A relative Frobenius guarantee therefore need not provide a relative spectral guarantee when many small singular values contribute to the total tail energy.

The survey presents a spectral approximation based on repeated matrix products, but its dependence on repeated passes and the target rank does not have the requested additive input-sparsity form. Its Frobenius result already achieves that form.

Bakshi, Bhattacharyya, Kannan, Woodruff and Zhou’s 2021 latent-simplex algorithm obtains input-sparsity time under a spectral-mass assumption. Their paper connects removal of that assumption to a breakthrough for spectral low-rank approximation, rather than claiming to solve the unrestricted matrix problem.

A bound of the form input size plus a polynomial in rank and accuracy times n matters especially when a large sparse matrix can be read once but cannot cheaply be multiplied by many vectors. The additive second term also accommodates the n-by-k output. No explicit n-by-n projection is requested.
